summary: Defines MIB objects that allow delegation of management scripts to distributed managers.

eli5.summary: It lets a boss hand a to-do script to helpers near the machines.

questions: how do you push a script with snmp
what is a launch button in the script mib
how does the script mib control access
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a manager send management scripts to helper managers, run them and collect the results.

tldr.problem: Managing a large network from one central point is heavy, so management functions are better delegated to distributed managers near the devices, which needs a standard way to ship and control scripts.
tldr.mechanism: The Script MIB defines SNMP tables for the languages a system supports, the scripts it holds, the script code, launch buttons that start scripts, and the runs in progress or recently finished.
tldr.outcome: A manager can transfer a script by push or pull, start, suspend, resume or abort it, and collect results later. RFC 3165 obsoletes RFC 2592.

today: RFC 3165 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2001. It obsoletes RFC 2592, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Script MIB Does
sections.content:
The Script MIB module is used to delegate management functions to distributed managers. The functions are management scripts written in a management scripting language. The MIB makes no assumption about the language and even allows compiled native code, if the implementation can run it under the control of this MIB.

It provides capabilities to transfer scripts to a distributed manager, to initiate, suspend, resume and terminate them, to pass arguments, to monitor and control running scripts, and to transfer their results. The RFC states it does not address the generation of notifications or how a Script MIB implementation addresses remote agents.

The module is written in SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP like any other MIB.
sections.eli5: It is a set of standard buttons and slots: put a script in, press start, pause or stop it, and read what came out.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A distributed manager is a processing entity that performs network management functions and is assumed to implement the Script MIB. A higher-level manager, or just manager, is an entity or human who initiates and controls the work of one or more distributed managers.

A distributed manager splits into an SNMP entity that implements the Script MIB and a runtime system that executes scripts. The MIB treats the runtime system as the managed resource it controls.

A launch button is the conceptual button used to start a script. It assigns control parameters to the script and defines the ownership of scripts started from it, which the runtime system can use to enforce security profiles.
sections.eli5: The boss is the manager, the helper is the distributed manager, and the launch button is the start button that also says whose permissions the script uses.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The Script MIB must not assume any specific language or runtime system, must help avoid new management problems such as script version problems, must provide SNMP interfaces to all functions needed to delegate scripts, and must be organized so that view-based access control can be applied effectively. Other protocols may be used in addition if they offer a significant improvement in convenience or performance.

Languages are identified by an object identifier, with well-known languages registered by IANA. A language version number, an object identifier for the implementing organization and an implementation version number let a manager decide whether a script can run on a given system. A separate table lists language extensions, such as libraries for sending SNMP requests.

Scripts reach a distributed manager by the push model (the manager writes the script with a sequence of SNMP set requests, in fragments if needed) or the pull model (the manager writes a URL and the distributed manager fetches the script, for example by FTP or HTTP). Built-in scripts are also allowed, and implementing push or pull is not required.

Script arguments and results are OCTET STRING values. A runtime error terminates the script, and an exit code and human readable error message are left in the MIB. A notification with the exit code, message and timestamp is generated when a script ends with an error exit code. A history of finished scripts stays in the MIB for later collection.
sections.eli5: Scripts can come by hand-delivery (push) or the helper can fetch them from an address (pull). Any language may be used, and every script gets a report card when it finishes.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The objects fall into five groups, each built around one table.

  • Language group (smLangTable, smExtsnTable): the languages and extensions an implementation supports.
  • Script group (smScriptTable): all known scripts. A script is loaded when smScriptAdminStatus is set to enabled, and smScriptOperStatus moves from retrieving to compiling to enabled, or to an error such as compilationFailed.
  • Code group (smCodeTable): script code that can be written and edited by SNMP sets, fragmented across rows. Editing is only possible while smScriptOperStatus is editing. This group is optional.
  • Launch group (smLaunchTable): launch buttons that tie a script to an owner, arguments and limits such as how many copies may run at once.
  • Run group (smRunTable): scripts running or recently terminated, with argument, result, exit code, state and timestamps.

Three smRunTable objects are writable: smRunLifeTime (maximum running time before the script is terminated), smRunExpireTime (how long a finished run stays in the table) and smRunControl (suspend, resume or abort).
sections.eli5: There are five tables, like five drawers: what languages exist, which scripts are stored, the script text, the start buttons, and the list of jobs running or just finished.

sections.title: Delegating and Controlling Scripts
sections.content:
Section 7 walks through the normal steps. To push a script, the manager checks the language tables, creates a row in smScriptTable with smScriptRowStatus set to createAndWait and an empty smScriptSource, activates the row and sets the admin status to editing, fills smCodeTable, sets the admin status to enabled, and polls smScriptOperStatus until it is enabled or an error. To pull, the manager puts a URL in smScriptSource and enables the script.

To launch, the manager creates a launch button row, then writes a value to smLaunchStart. A new smRunTable row appears, and the manager polls smRunState for executing, suspended or terminated. Setting smRunControl or smLaunchControl to suspend, resume or abort controls one run or all runs from a button.

Setting smRunLifeTime to zero terminates a script with a lifeTimeExceeded exit code. A manager can keep the lifetime short and extend it periodically, so scripts end by themselves if contact is lost. Setting smRunExpireTime to 0 removes a terminated run.
sections.eli5: To use a script you hand it over, press enable, then press start and keep checking the status light until it says running or done.

sections.title: Access Control and Security
sections.content:
Section 8 shows how the View-based Access Control Model (VACM) can be configured. Because the first index of the tables is an owner (an SnmpAdminString), VACM views can give a group access to only its own entries. Examples include a sandbox for the "guest" group, sharing a repository of scripts owned by "utils" between "junior" and "senior" groups, and letting "junior" start scripts that run with the permissions of an "emergency" owner.

The Security Considerations section warns that read-write and read-create objects may be sensitive, and that SNMPv1 by itself is not secure. It recommends the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model and VACM. Because the MIB distributes applications in arbitrary languages to remote systems, the security features of the available languages should be considered. Access control on URLs, especially the file scheme, must be handled by the operating system, and the owner index should be mapped to a local user identity.
sections.eli5: Because scripts can do real work, each owner gets only their own drawers, and strong login checks are recommended.

sections.title: IANA Language Registry
sections.content: IANA maintains a MIB module, IANA-LANGUAGE-MIB, that provides object identifier registrations for well-known languages, to reduce interoperability problems. Languages can still be registered in private OID spaces, which is attractive for experimental languages. Additions or changes to the IANA list require Designated Expert Review.
sections.eli5: There is a public list of well-known script languages, but you may keep a private list for your own.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2592
sections.content:
RFC 3165 updates the boilerplate and references, fixes typos and adds clarifications reported by implementors. New objects include smScriptError, smLaunchError, smScriptLastChange, smLaunchLastChange, smLaunchRowExpireTime, smRunResultTime and smRunErrorTime.

Setting smRunLifeTime to its maximum value now disables the timer so scripts can run forever. An autostart value was added to smLaunchAdminStatus, and an expired state to smLaunchOperStatus. A smScriptException notification was added, and several compliance and group definitions were deprecated and replaced by new versions.
sections.eli5: This version adds more status slots, a way to let a job run forever, an auto-start option, and fixes unclear wording.
